content: Switching therapy for individuals on NNRTI-based regimens was specifically evaluated, excluding those on dolutegravir (DTG) or protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimens. Data from nine national surveys assessing acquired drug resistance in adults after a single elevated viral load result revealed that resistance to NNRTIs ranged from 50% in Eswatini to 97% in Uganda at 12 months post-ART initiation. At 48 months or later, resistance prevalence ranged from 71% in Nicaragua to 92% in Senegal. However, these findings had wide confidence intervals. Two studies reviewed drug resistance among adults on TDF combined with lamivudine or emtricitabine (FTC) and efavirenz (EFV) in lowand middle-income countries. Between 1998 and 2015, NNRTI resistance mutations at treatment failure ranged from 42% in Eastern Africa to 82% in Western and Central Africa, with Southern Africa showing a mid-range resistance of 59%. Children and adolescents on NNRTI-based regimens exhibited particularly high levels of drug resistance. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that 46% of individuals on NNRTI-based first-line ART achieved viral suppression after an elevated viral load, suggesting poor adherence in many cases. Suppression rates were lower among children (31%) and adolescents (40%) compared to adults (50%). Surveys indicated that people living with HIV preferred achieving viral suppression over time. Cost-effectiveness modeling suggested that switching adults from NNRTI-based ART to second-line therapy after a single elevated viral load (>1000 copies/mL) could improve health outcomes, reduce HIV transmission, and lower mortality, particularly for those with drug resistance. This intervention was cost-effective at a threshold of $500 per DALY averted, though some individuals without resistance might be unnecessarily switched. Data suggest that a significant proportion (40–97%) of individuals in lowand middle-income countries on NNRTI-based ART with a single elevated viral load have drug resistance and would benefit from switching to second-line ART. However, adherence counseling and repeat viral load testing are often underutilized, with fewer than 25% receiving follow-up testing. Rapid therapy switching for NNRTI-based regimens could reduce further drug resistance and transmission risks, especially in pregnant and breastfeeding women. However, 30–40% of individuals with elevated viral loads may not have drug resistance, leading to unnecessary therapy changes. An immediate switch algorithm could expedite treatment failure identification, but clinical support is essential for timely transitions to second-line ART. Strengthening adherence counseling during ART initiation and throughout treatment is critical, particularly after elevated viral load results. The WHO recommends maintaining the treatment failure threshold at 1000 copies/mL, with viral suppression defined as ≤50 copies/mL. Low-level viremia (50–1000 copies/mL) is associated with future virological failure, particularly at levels between 200–500 copies/mL. Studies show that detectable viral loads under 1000 copies/mL can lead to new drug resistance mutations. However, the clinical relevance of low-level viremia for individuals on DTGor PI-based regimens remains unclear. Regarding HIV transmission, low-level viremia (<1000 copies/mL) was not linked to sexual transmission. Vertical transmission risks were observed even at low viral loads, though at low proportions. No studies evaluated HIV transmissibility through shared drug injection equipment at viral loads under 1000 copies/mL. Implementation considerations include expanding access to viral load testing through dried blood spots, point-of-care technologies, or alternative specimen types. Diagnostic accuracy for detecting treatment failure at lower thresholds varied across technologies, with some achieving sensitivity and specificity above 90%. Training healthcare providers on ART, treatment failure, therapy switching, and adherence support is essential. For pregnant and breastfeeding women, same-day point-of-care viral load testing is recommended to expedite clinical decisions and prevent transmission. Enhanced adherence counseling should be provided at all antenatal and postnatal visits. Viral load testing at 34–36 weeks of gestation or delivery is advised to identify women at risk of treatment failure and perinatal transmission. Infants of mothers with elevated viral loads (>1000 copies/mL) should receive enhanced postnatal prophylaxis and, where available, nucleic acid testing at birth. Research gaps include understanding the relationship between low-level viremia and drug resistance development for DTG and other optimized ARVs, as well as the role of drug resistance testing in treatment failure algorithms for DTG-based regimens. Additional data on children and adolescents would support optimized treatment monitoring in these populations. Evidence is also limited on the ideal treatment monitoring algorithm for pregnant and breastfeeding women on ART.
